title: Chapter 11 — Data Analysis and Displays (40 Cards)

cards.front: What is a [[kw:measure of center]]?
cards.back: A value that represents the center, or typical value, of a data set. The mean, median, and mode are measures of center.

cards.front: Define the [[kw:mean]] of a numerical data set.
cards.back: The sum of the data values divided by the number of values. Symbol: $\bar{x}$ (x‑bar). Example: For 3,5,7, mean = (3+5+7)/3 = 5.

cards.front: Define the [[kw:median]] of a numerical data set.
cards.back: The middle number when the values are ordered. For an even number of values, it's the mean of the two middle numbers.

cards.front: Define the [[kw:mode]] of a data set.
cards.back: The value or values that occur most often. There can be one mode, more than one mode, or no mode.

cards.front: What is an [[kw:outlier]]?
cards.back: A data value that is much greater or much less than the other values in a data set. Example: \$16.50 in a set of wages around \$8–\$9.

cards.front: How does an outlier affect the mean and median?
cards.back: It pulls the [[imp:mean]] toward it (large effect). It has [[imp:little effect]] on the median, because the median depends only on the middle position.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:measure of variation]]?
cards.back: A measure that describes the spread, or distribution, of a data set. Examples: range and standard deviation.

cards.front: Define the [[kw:range]] of a data set.
cards.back: The difference between the greatest and least values. Range = max − min. Example: 19,20,…,48 → range = 48−19 = 29.

cards.front: What is the [[kw:standard deviation]]?
cards.back: A measure of how much a typical value differs from the mean. Symbol: $\sigma$ (sigma). A small $\sigma$ means data are clustered around the mean; a large $\sigma$ means data are more spread out.

cards.front: Outline the steps to compute standard deviation.
cards.back: 1. Find the mean $\bar{x}$. 2. Find each deviation $x-\bar{x}$. 3. Square each deviation. 4. Find the mean of the squared deviations (variance). 5. Take the square root.

cards.front: What happens to the mean and standard deviation if you add a constant $k$ to every value?
cards.back: The mean, median, and mode all increase by $k$. The range and standard deviation [[imp:do not change]] (the spread stays the same).

cards.front: What happens to the mean and standard deviation if you multiply every value by a constant $k > 0$?
cards.back: All measures of center (mean, median, mode) and measures of variation (range, standard deviation) are [[imp:multiplied by $k$]].

cards.front: When is the median a better measure of center than the mean?
cards.back: When the data set contains outliers or is skewed. The median is resistant to extreme values and better represents the typical value.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:box-and-whisker plot]]?
cards.back: A data display that shows the variability of a data set along a number line using the five-number summary: minimum, Q1, median, Q3, maximum.

cards.front: What is the [[kw:five-number summary]]?
cards.back: The five key values that make up a box-and-whisker plot: least value, first quartile (Q1), median (Q2), third quartile (Q3), greatest value.

cards.front: Define [[kw:quartiles]].
cards.back: Values that divide an ordered data set into four equal parts. Q1 is the median of the lower half, Q2 is the overall median, Q3 is the median of the upper half.

cards.front: How is the first quartile (Q1) found?
cards.back: Q1 is the median of the lower half of the ordered data. If the overall median falls on a data value, exclude it from both halves.

cards.front: What is the [[kw:interquartile range (IQR)]]?
cards.back: The difference between the third quartile and the first quartile: $$\text{IQR} = Q_3 - Q_1$$ It measures the spread of the middle 50% of the data.

cards.front: What percentage of the data lies in each whisker of a box-and-whisker plot?
cards.back: About 25% of the data lies in each whisker. The box contains the middle 50% of the data.

cards.front: How can you tell if a distribution is [[imp:skewed left]] from a box-and-whisker plot?
cards.back: The left whisker is longer than the right whisker. Most of the data are on the right side of the plot.

cards.front: How can you tell if a distribution is [[imp:skewed right]] from a box-and-whisker plot?
cards.back: The right whisker is longer than the left whisker. Most of the data are on the left side of the plot.

cards.front: What does a symmetric box-and-whisker plot look like?
cards.back: The whiskers are about the same length, and the median is centered in the middle of the box.

cards.front: Describe a [[kw:symmetric]] distribution from a histogram.
cards.back: The right side of the histogram is approximately a mirror image of the left side. The mean and median are about equal.

cards.front: Describe a [[kw:skewed left]] distribution from a histogram.
cards.back: The tail of the histogram extends to the left. Most of the data are on the right. The mean is usually less than the median.

cards.front: Describe a [[kw:skewed right]] distribution from a histogram.
cards.back: The tail of the histogram extends to the right. Most of the data are on the left. The mean is usually greater than the median.

cards.front: For a symmetric distribution, which measures of center and spread should you use?
cards.back: Use the [[imp:mean]] to describe the center and the [[imp:standard deviation]] to describe the spread.

cards.front: For a skewed distribution, which measures of center and spread should you use?
cards.back: Use the [[imp:median]] to describe the center and the [[imp:five-number summary]] to describe the spread.

cards.front: State the [[kw:Empirical Rule]] for bell‑shaped distributions.
cards.back: About 68% of data lie within 1 SD of the mean. About 95% lie within 2 SDs. About 99.7% lie within 3 SDs. Only applies to bell‑shaped, symmetric data.

cards.front: When is a data value considered unusual in a bell‑shaped distribution?
cards.back: When it lies more than [[imp:2 standard deviations]] from the mean. About 95% of data lie within 2 SDs.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:two-way table]]?
cards.back: A frequency table that displays data collected from one source that belong to two different categories. One category is represented by rows and the other by columns.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:joint frequency]]?
cards.back: Each entry inside a two-way table. It counts how many individuals fall into both a specific row category and a specific column category.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:marginal frequency]]?
cards.back: The sum of the joint frequencies in a row or a column. They appear in the 'Total' row and 'Total' column.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:joint relative frequency]]?
cards.back: The ratio of a joint frequency to the grand total. It tells what fraction or percent of the whole group falls into a specific cell.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:conditional relative frequency]]?
cards.back: The ratio of a joint frequency to a marginal frequency (row or column total). It tells what fraction or percent of a subgroup falls into a specific cell.

cards.front: How do you check for an [[kw:association]] between two variables in a two-way table?
cards.back: Compute conditional relative frequencies (based on row or column totals) and compare them. If they are very different, there is an association.

cards.front: What is [[kw:qualitative data]]?
cards.back: Data that consist of labels or nonnumerical entries that can be separated into categories. Also called categorical data. Examples: eye color, jersey numbers, types of flowers.

cards.front: What is [[kw:quantitative data]]?
cards.back: Data that consist of numbers representing counts or measurements. You can perform arithmetic operations and find a mean. Examples: heights, prices, ages, test scores.

cards.front: What type of graph is best for displaying qualitative data as parts of a whole?
cards.back: A [[imp:circle graph]] (pie chart). It shows the proportion of each category relative to the total.

cards.front: What type of graph is best for showing the distribution of quantitative data in intervals?
cards.back: A [[imp:histogram]]. It is a bar graph where the bars touch, showing how data are spread across equal intervals.

cards.front: What is a [[kw:misleading graph]]?
cards.back: A statistical graph that is not drawn appropriately, often giving viewers a false impression. Common issues: scale does not start at zero, uneven increments, missing labels.
